title: Lasting pain after shingles
intro: Some people continue to have burning or stabbing pain in the skin area where shingles occurred, long after the rash has healed. This is called postherpetic neuralgia. It is more common in older people and can last months or longer, but treatments can reduce the pain and help you function.

sections.heading: What happens
paragraphs: Shingles is caused by reactivation of the chickenpox virus, which can damage nerves. After the blisters heal, the damaged nerves may keep sending pain signals. Pain is generally defined as postherpetic when it persists for at least three months after the rash started.

sections.heading: Who is at risk
paragraphs: The risk increases with age, with severe pain or an extensive rash during the acute illness, and with weak immunity. Starting antiviral medicine early after the rash appears may lower the chance of long-lasting pain, which is one reason to see a doctor quickly if you suspect shingles.

sections.heading: How it feels
paragraphs: People describe burning, aching, stabbing or electric-shock pain, sensitivity to light touch such as clothing, and itching or numbness. The pain can disturb sleep, mood and daily activities, and can lead to tiredness and withdrawal from social life.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Ordinary painkillers often do not help nerve pain. Medicines used include certain anticonvulsants and antidepressants taken in low doses, which are increased gradually, as well as capsaicin or lidocaine patches applied to the skin. Opioids are rarely used and carry risks. Side effects such as drowsiness and dizziness should be discussed. Pain clinics offer further options such as nerve blocks.
Combining medicine with physical activity, relaxation, good sleep and psychological support can help you cope. Loose, soft clothing and cooling may ease sensitive skin.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: A vaccine against shingles is recommended in many countries for older adults and some younger people at risk. It reduces the chance of shingles and also of lasting nerve pain. Ask your doctor whether vaccination is advisable for you.

examples.title: Describing the pain
examples.text: Imagine you still have burning pain on your chest wall months after shingles. You could keep a diary of pain levels and triggers and discuss with your doctor which nerve pain medicine to try first.

examples.title: Asking about vaccination
examples.text: Suppose a relative recently had shingles and you are over 60. You might ask your doctor about the shingles vaccine and whether you would need more than one dose.
